title: The Joker Jackpot: Why Math Makes Dealers Lucky
text:
The Math
There are 8 jokers in the 152 tiles, which means every time you pick up a tile, you have a 5.3% shot at drawing a joker - and that percentage never changes regardless of what you’ve drawn before.

8/152 = 5.3%

But here’s the question every player really wants answered: If I don’t have jokers now, what are my chances of getting them as I draw more tiles?
Important: This isn’t about being “due” for a joker, each individual draw is still 5.3%. This is about the cumulative effect of getting multiple chances.
Let’s track your cumulative odds of finding at least one joker.
Aside: The dealer gets a small but real advantage – the fact that they start with 14 tiles in the opening deal versus 13 for everyone else bumps their “at least one joker” odds from 52% to 55%, a ~3 percentage point edge that persists throughout the game.

rounds <- 1:25
joker_prob_per_tile <- 8/152  

prob_at_least_one_cumulative <- 1 - (1 - joker_prob_per_tile)^rounds

cumulative_data <- data.frame(
  round = rounds,
  tiles_drawn = rounds,
  probability = prob_at_least_one_cumulative,
  percentage = paste0(round(prob_at_least_one_cumulative * 100, 1), "%")
)


ggplot(cumulative_data, aes(x = round, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(size = 2, color = "#E8A8D3", lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#E8A8D3") +
  geom_text(data = cumulative_data[c(5, 10, 15, 20), ],
            aes(label = percentage), 
            vjust = -1.5, size = 5, fontface = "bold", color = "#34495E") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent,
                     limits = c(0, 1),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, 5)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 20, color = "#34495E"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#34495E"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(color = "#0085FF", linewidth = 5),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 13, color = "#E8A8D3", hjust = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Turns Played",
    y = "Chance of Getting At Least One Joker",
    caption = "Created by: Mahj Math"
  )

title: The Joker Jackpot: Why Math Makes Dealers Lucky
text:
Why It Matters
The patience payoff is real. If you start with zero jokers, you hit 50% odds of finding at least one by around round 13.
This doesn’t mean you’re “due” for a joker by round 14. Each tile you draw is still independently 5.3% likely to be a joker. The cumulative probability just reflects getting multiple independent chances.

title: The Joker Jackpot: Why Math Makes Dealers Lucky
text:
Simple Strategy
Don’t confuse cumulative odds with individual odds: Just because you have >50% cumulative chase by round 14 doesn’t mean your next tile is more likely to be a joker. It’s still exactly 5.3%, same as always.
Early game (Rounds 1-5): If you started with zero jokers, resist the urge to pivot your entire strategy. The cumulative math shows you’re building toward better odds, but you’re not “due” for anything.
Mid game (Rounds 6-12): This is decision time. You’ve had many independent chances at jokers by now. If you still don’t have any, start considering joker-independent hands.
Late game (Rounds 13+): Don’t chase jokers desperately thinking you “deserve” them after bad luck. Each remaining tile is still just 5.3% likely to be a joker, regardless of your previous draws.
The dealer advantage is small but real: Over 100 games as dealer, you’ll average about 3 extra jokers total compared to regular players. Don’t change your fundamental strategy, but acknowledge the slight edge.

title: The Joker Jackpot: Why Math Makes Dealers Lucky
text:
The Key Insight
Cumulative probability shows you’re getting multiple independent chances at jokers, not that you’re “due” for them. Each tile is still 5.3%, but having many chances improves your overall odds of success. Use this to set realistic expectations about when to pivot strategies, not to justify risky late-game chasing.

title: 5 and 6: The Hot Tiles
text:
Out of the 55 lines on your 2025 card there are 1,002 unique hands (curious about why? Check out our unique hands post). Each of these has 14 tiles:

14 x 1,002 = 14,028 winning tiles

We can count how many times 5 and 6 appear in these 14,028 winning tiles.

5s appear in 1,380 hands
6s appear in 1,440 hands




1,380 / 14,028 = 9.8% 5s



1,440 / 14,028 = 10.3% 6s



5 and 6 are statistically the most in demand tiles!

Next time you’re dealt middle numbers, remember: you’re holding the most wanted tiles at the table.

title: Charleston Strategy: Pass Smart, Not Hard
text:
Why this matters
If you don’t have clear strategy on hand, here are some helpful general rules you can follow during Charleston.

✅ KEEP: 3, 5, 6, F
These appear in 9-10% of winning hands. Hold onto them unless you’re certain about your direction.


🤔 MAYBE KEEP: 2, 4, 7, 8, 9
Mid-demand tiles (6-8%). Good to keep if they fit your emerging pattern.


❌ SAFE TO PASS: Winds
Winds are not in as many hands this season. Consider passing these first unless you have a clear path to victory with them.

title: Charleston Strategy: Pass Smart, Not Hard
text:
💡 Pro Tip
Flowers appear in more winning hands than any number except 5 and 6.

The 2025 Reality: Keep in mind others at the table may be thinking about this too, while everyone fights over 5s and 6s, you might find more success building toward hands that use the mid-range numbers (2, 4, 7, 8, 9) that others are passing.

title: 1 is The Loneliest Number
text:
Why This Matters
While everyone fights over 5s and 6s (each around 10% of the winning tiles), sweet little 1 sits quietly at just 4% - less than half the demand of the popular middle numbers. When you’re deciding between potential hands during gameplay you could:
✅ Target lines that include 1s - you’ll have less competition
✅ Pivot to 1-heavy strategies when middle numbers are scarce
